newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine shelves plans to limit foreign T-bill buys.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine shelves plans to limit foreign T-bill buys.

text.p: Ukraine has quietly shelved plans to limit foreign buying on its lucrative Treasury bill (T-bill) market, but on Thursday the central bank showed it had a watchful eye on the process by telling banks to register all non-resident deals.

"The suggested law was considered to be inconsistent with Ukrainian law and was rejected by the Justice Ministry. This happened recently," one Western expert, who asked to not be named, said without specifying when the decision was taken.

Top central bank and Finance Ministry officials proposed a new law last month to curb foreign buying, estimated to occupy at least half of a market which has become attractive due to a stable currency and slowed inflation.
Ukrainian dealers say non-residents are so active on the T-bill market that they have helped push up the rate of the hryvnia, which has been firming steadily for three weeks.
It has come very close to the 1.76 rate at which it was introduced last September, rising to 1.7650 to the dollar on the Ukraine Interbank Currency Exchange on Thursday from 1.8500 on Monday.
Bankers said non-residents would not be deterred by the new instruction sent to banks on Thursday.
Banks received an instruction by electronic mail from the central bank telling them to register all non-resident T-bill deals within three days, starting from February 25.
One Western banker, who asked not to be named, said the move originated from a law passed last year ordering the registration of foreign investment deals three days after signing.
"So far it was unclear whether foreign T-bill purchases also had to be registered. This means the central bank has a 100 percent overview of all participation," he said.
The banker said the new rule would probably not impede foreigners from buying T-bills, on which Ukraine relies heavily to finance its deficit. "It's a very lucrative market," he said.
"It is only a matter of re-organisation. But there are no limitations," another Western banker said.

Three- and six-month discount T-bills fetched yields of around 30 percent this week, and nine- and 12-month papers were around 40 percent. The central bank auctions the securities, usually twice weekly, on the ministry's behalf.

An economist said the bank and ministry could still attempt to revive the law limiting foreign participation, which required Justice Ministry permission to be passed, but said Western advisers would be strongly opposed.
"This would be something a lot of people would be telling them not to do," he said. "There will be a lot of high-level policy advice about this being a mistake."
But another Western expert suggested Ukraine would eventually need to limit foreign involvement to protect itself from money moving rapidly in and out of the country.

Economists have estimated that Ukraine would issue 2.5 trillion hryvnia ($1.3 trillion) worth of paper to cover the 1997 deficit, but the final figure will not be known until the budget is passed in March or April.
Dealers have said the biggest foreign buyers of T-bills, first issued in March 1995, were Credit Suisse's CS First Boston, Societe Generale and Credit Lyonnais .
Ukrainian media reported recently that Chase Manhattan Corporation had also become involved.
Banks in Cyprus and the Baltic states, probably handling Russian money, are also big investors, dealers said.
